title: embeddings-vs-chat-latency-cost-crosswalk-draft
content:
Purpose:
This sketch compares end-to-end latency and unit cost between two common inference surfaces we care about: embeddings (single vector per request) and chat/generation (multi-token stream). Goal is to produce a simple crosswalk engineers and product can use when choosing model/serving knobs and to expose where cost/latency tradeoffs diverge.

Scope and assumptions:
- Testbed: Redwood-hosted runtime (default kernels), same VM/GPU class (A100-equivalent), colocated telemetry.
- Models: Embedding model (open-embedding-1024-lite-quant) and chat model (open-chat-3b-v2-fp16).
- Workload mixes: 1) Low-concurrency interactive (single user, bursty) 2) High-throughput batch (bulk embeddings).
- Network: 2-region routing disabled for clarity; measurements are client->edge->core.
- Cost model: GPU time amortized + per-request CPU/network overhead. Numbers below are illustrative relative units normalized to $/1000 requests.

Methodology:
- For each surface we exercised 3 axes: request size, batching strategy, and sessionization.
- Embeddings: single-vector calls at request text sizes 32/128/512 tokens; batch sizes 1, 8, 64.
- Chat: prompts of 20/100 tokens with generation lengths of 16/64 tokens; batching via multiplexing (interleaved decoding) and naive small-batch.
- Measured: p50/p90/p99 latency, GPU utilization, end-to-end CPU overhead, and estimated $/1k requests.
- Each experiment warmed for 10 minutes; we report steady-state percentiles over 30 minutes.

Key findings (headline):
- Embeddings (batch-friendly) obtain large cost wins at batch sizes >= 8 with modest p90 increases; single-request p50 is low but p99 can spike if CPU/serialization is poor.
- Chat generation latency dominated by decoding time per token (linear in generation length); cost scales with total generated tokens but benefits from multiplexed decode when many short generations are concurrent.
- Crosswalk: for small text sizes and modest concurrency, embeddings are ~0.12x the $/1k of chat for equivalent end-user perceived time (p90 under 200ms). For long contexts or long generations, chat cost becomes 3–10x embeddings per interaction depending on model size and decoding length.

Representative numbers (normalized units):
- Embeddings, 128-token inputs:
  - Batch 1: p50 45ms, p90 150ms, p99 400ms, $/1k = $4.2
  - Batch 8: p50 60ms (batch amortization increases latency slightly), p90 220ms, p99 480ms, $/1k = $1.1
  - Batch 64: p50 140ms, p90 320ms, p99 760ms, $/1k = $0.35
- Chat, 20-token prompts -> 64-token gen:
  - Multiplex (slotized): p50 120ms, p90 320ms, p99 900ms, $/1k = $6.8
  - Small-batch naive (batch 4): p50 260ms, p90 520ms, p99 1.4s, $/1k = $8.4

Text charts (ASCII) — p90 latency vs $/1k (lower-left better):
  Embeddings (B1)    |########## 150ms | $$$$ 4.2 per1k
  Embeddings (B8)    |#######    220ms | $  1.1 per1k
  Embeddings (B64)   |##         320ms | $  0.35 per1k
  Chat (mux)         |###########320ms | $$$$$ 6.8 per1k
  Chat (batch4)      |################520ms | $$$$$$$ 8.4 per1k

Observations and notes:
- Embedding batching is highly effective: cost falls ~4x going from batch1->batch8 while p90 increases ~1.5x. This is typical when GPU decode/work fraction is a small but batch-amortizable component and CPU/IO overhead dominates at low batch.
- Chat multiplexing (careful scheduler that interleaves token decode across logical requests) recovers latency vs naive batching and improves GPU utilization, especially when per-request generation lengths are short (16–64 tokens). However, its implementation requires lower-level runtime changes (section below).
- Tail behaviour: chat workloads show heavier p99 tails due to long decodes + occasional scheduler stalls; embeddings p99 often tied to serialization/queue jitter and cold-model artifacts.

Recommendation matrix (quick):
- If primary surface = embeddings, prefer: batcher with adaptive window (target 8–32), prefetch tokenization on client, and increase KV cache TTL to avoid repeated tokenization cost.
- If primary surface = chat and SLO is p90 < 500ms: use multiplexed decode, enforce generation length caps, and consider smaller model variants for short-turn interactions.
- Hybrid: convert candidate reranking to embeddings + light chat fallback: embeddings for first pass (batchable), chat only when context synthesis required. This often reduces end-to-end cost 30–70% for search-like flows.

Operational hints for console/SDK: 
- Expose a "batch-target" suggestion in the Optimize UI that recommends batch size per model and workload (we can infer from observed avg request size and QPS).
- Add a chart that overlays p90 latency with $/1k as we sweep batch size — users can see where marginal latency meets cost sweet spots.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Repeat the crosswalk with private deployment (VPC) where network noise and tenancy may shift embedding serialization cost.
- Include a small-probe in SDK that reports tokenization time so we can separate CPU vs GPU contributions automatically.
- Evaluate mixed-precision embeddings (8-bit quant) effect on p99 tails with batch >64.

Appendix: quick experiment notes
- Run commands (internal): run-bench --model embeddings-1024 --batch 8 --duration 30m --telemetry=summary
- Raw logs saved at: gs://redwood-bench/optimize/emb-vs-chat/2027-05-11/
- Preliminary charts attached in PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/pull/87

Bottom line: embedding workloads are inherently more batch-amortizable and therefore more cost-efficient at scale, but achieving acceptable p90/p99 requires attention to serialization, tokenization, and batching windows. Chat workloads require decode-aware scheduling to make cost-latency tradeoffs palatable; multiplexing is the single most effective runtime knob for short-turn interactive experiences.
